title: Tested, not vibed: GTM writing evals
tagline: Testing whether the instructions behind AI-written GTM copy beat saying nothing, with every room attended debriefed into the graph behind it.
why: The pipeline writes every post, note and brief from a style guide of more than 100 rules, and none of them has ever been run against a no-guidance control, so nobody can say which rules change the output. Debriefs lag too: most attended rooms never got a post-event brief, so the graph holds a fraction of what was heard.
mission: A public, re-runnable eval suite for GTM agent writing. It screens failure types from Alex's own review comments against a no-guidance control, then tests rule wordings only where the control fails. Alongside it: a backfill of every undebriefed attended room, and an audit of the whole rulebook.
destination: A pre-registered study with raw samples, grader code and outside graders, published so a stranger can re-run it. The rulebook keeps only rules that beat saying nothing, and at least 50 attended rooms are debriefed into the graph. Anyone can check by re-running the suite and reading the coverage count.
showcase: Designing a behaviour eval the way a lab would: pre-registration before the first sample, a no-guidance control, yes/no graders, a rep count chosen for statistical power, and every raw sample published
Running a falsification search before claiming a 'first', then narrowing the claim to what the prior-art search left standing
Re-deriving a cited number from the raw labels before relying on it, and correcting the record when the two disagreed
Sizing a build by two budgets: the hours only Alex can give (decisions, labels, reads) and the hours agents can run overnight
Applying a method from software engineering (test the instruction against its absence first) to sales and marketing writing

decisions.decision: Adopt the testing method, not the borrowed skills: an instruction stays only if it beats saying nothing.
decisions.why: Imported skills were written for coding agents. The method transfers to writing, the wording doesn't.

decisions.decision: Screen many failure types against a control instead of hand-picking two test cases.
decisions.why: Picking the cases yourself biases the study, and two small cases make the whole result hang on chance.

decisions.decision: Backfilled debriefs write to the knowledge graph without step-by-step review. Drafts, outreach and CRM records stay out of the backfill.
decisions.why: Lead with building and add controls when a real failure shows up.

decisions.decision: Narrow the headline from 'first eval of GTM agent writing' to 'first head-to-head test of marketplace GTM skills against a no-guidance control, blind and independently graded'.
decisions.why: A prior-art search found a public single-skill comparison and a public sales-outreach benchmark, so the broad claim wouldn't hold.

open.question: Final sign-off on the five-lane plan, so the per-lane work can be opened.

Name and home of the public eval-suite repo.

risks.risk: The subscription may not sustain the sampling rate the study needs. The rate hasn't been measured yet.
risks.mitigation: A timed 100-sample throughput test in week 1, with a set order of what gets cut if the rate binds. The study itself is cut last.

risks.risk: The author wrote the rules, the failure cases and the grader, so a positive result could just be the author agreeing with himself.
risks.mitigation: By design: pre-registration before the first sample, yes/no checks graded by code where possible, a blind grader that never sees the style guide, raw samples published, and outside graders whose agreement is reported.

risks.risk: Backfilled debriefs written weeks after the event could read as fact to later runs.
risks.mitigation: By design, every backfilled claim is tagged as backfill, and nothing public is written from a backfilled event.
